title: Step 1 · QC & host removal with VANISH
text:
Before you count resistance genes, clean the reads. VANISH does two things in one pass: it quality-controls every read (with fastp) and then makes the host DNA vanish (with bowtie2). What comes out is quality-trimmed, host-free FASTQ — ready for ResScan.
First, switch on the VANISH environment:

title: Step 1 · QC & host removal with VANISH
text:
1a · Prepare the read list
VANISH needs a small CSV pairing each sample’s forward and reverse files. vanish-prep builds it automatically — point it at the reads and tell it how the mates are named (_1 / _2):
vanish-prep --fastq_dir data/rawdata_10K --r1 "_1" --r2 "_2" --out read_pairs.csv
Have a look — one row per sample, forward and reverse:
cat read_pairs.csv






A ready-made copy also ships at data/read_pairs.csv, so you can skip this step if you like — they’re identical.

title: Step 1 · QC & host removal with VANISH
text:
1b · Run VANISH
Now dehost and QC all 36 samples. We point --host_index at the toy human index that shipped with the repo, and keep --cpus modest for a laptop:
vanish --read_pairs read_pairs.csv \
       --fastq_dir data/rawdata_10K \
       --host_index data/host_index/toy_human \
       --cpus 4
On this 10K subset it finishes in a minute or two. You’ll see Nextflow tick through the three stages:
 N E X T F L O W   ~  version 26.04.x
executor >  local

[..] FASTP_QC (SRR10842837)    [100%] 36 of 36 ✔
[..] REMOVE_HOST (SRR10842865) [100%] 36 of 36 ✔
[..] COMPILE_REPORT            [100%] 1 of 1  ✔

--- Vanish Run Complete ---
Status:   SUCCESS
Output:   vanished

title: Step 1 · QC & host removal with VANISH
text:
1c · See what happened
The cleaned reads keep their original names, under vanished/vanished_reads/:
ls vanished/vanished_reads/ | head
And a per-sample report tells you what was trimmed and removed — reads in, QC drops, host reads removed, reads out:
column -s, -t vanished/vanish_filtering_report.csv | head






WarningExpect almost no host removal here — that’s by design



Our toy index is only the human mitochondrion, so it catches just a trickle of host reads. The QC step is still doing real work. On real data with the full human index, host removal is typically substantial — which is exactly why this step matters.

title: Step 1 · QC & host removal with VANISH
text:
Tidy up (optional)
Nextflow keeps a work/ scratch directory that can balloon far beyond your input. Once you’ve seen the results, reclaim the space:
rm -rf work .nextflow*
Finally, leave the VANISH environment before moving on:
mamba deactivate
Cleaned reads in hand — on to Step 2.

title: Step 2 · Quantifying AMR with ResScan
text:
Now the clean reads meet the resistance database. ResScan maps each sample against CARD to find AMR genes, and against a set of universal single-copy bacterial genes to estimate how many bacterial cells were there — then divides one by the other to report RPKPMC, its preferred default metric: resistance-gene copies per bacterial cell.
We’ll do it twice: one sample by hand to see the shape of the output, then all 36 at once in batch mode.

title: Step 2 · Quantifying AMR with ResScan
text:
2a · One sample
Give ResScan the sample’s two vanished mate files (comma-separated), an output prefix, some threads, and the CARD database you built in Setup:
mkdir -p resscan_single
resscan -i vanished/vanished_reads/SRR10842836_1.fastq.gz,vanished/vanished_reads/SRR10842836_2.fastq.gz \
        -o resscan_single/SRR10842836 \
        -t 4 \
        --card resscan_CARD_v4.0.1
When it finishes, look at what it produced:
ls resscan_single/
The key file is SRR10842836_homscan.tsv in the SRR10842836 folder — one row per detected AMR gene, with all the normalised metrics (including the default RPKPMC) as columns. There’s also a VarScan table for point-mutation resistance and interactive HTML coverage plots.






TipWhat are all these files, columns, and metrics?



The output reference breaks down every file ResScan writes, what each column means, how to decode the metric names, and the one label worth understanding up front — multiple. Worth a look before you dive into the numbers.


That’s one sample. Doing it 36 times by hand would be tedious and error-prone — so ResScan ships a batch mode.

title: Step 2 · Quantifying AMR with ResScan
text:
2b · All 36 at once (batch mode)
resscan_batch runs ResScan across every sample listed in a samplesheet — a plain CSV that is both the batch’s input and a durable record of exactly what you ran (keep it with your results). Each line is one sample: its name, then its read file(s). We ship one ready to go — take a look:
head -3 data/samplesheet.csv
SRR10842836,vanished/vanished_reads/SRR10842836_1.fastq.gz,vanished/vanished_reads/SRR10842836_2.fastq.gz
SRR10842837,vanished/vanished_reads/SRR10842837_1.fastq.gz,vanished/vanished_reads/SRR10842837_2.fastq.gz
...
Each line is sample_id,R1,R2. Commas separate a run’s mates; semicolons separate runs — so a sample sequenced across two runs goes on one line as SAMPLE,run1_R1,run1_R2;run2_R1,run2_R2.






NoteList all of a sample’s reads together



Pooling every run for a sample is what makes the lateral coverage metric meaningful — a gene’s coverage along its length is only correct when the full set of that sample’s reads is considered at once. (This is the same -i format resscan uses for a single sample — see the ResScan README.)








Paths are relative to where you launch. The paths above are relative to your working directory (this repo’s root, where the vanished/ folder from Step 1 lives); resscan_batch resolves them for you. Absolute paths work too.









TipPrefer to build your own samplesheet?





The helper create_samplesheet_from_mapping stamps a samplesheet out of a simple sample_id,file_prefix mapping — e.g.
create_samplesheet_from_mapping --mapping data/sampleid2fileprefix.csv \
    --fastq-dir vanished/vanished_reads --out samplesheet.csv
Or just write the CSV by hand in the format above. Either way, the batch only ever reads the samplesheet.



Now run the whole batch on the shipped samplesheet. --parallel sets how many samples run at once and --threads how many cores each gets — tune both to your machine:
resscan_batch \
    --samplesheet data/samplesheet.csv \
    --card resscan_CARD_v4.0.1 \
    --out SinkReplacementBatch \
    --parallel 4 \
    --threads 2
 N E X T F L O W   ~  version 26.04.x
executor >  local

[..] RESSCAN (SRR10842854) [100%] 36 of 36 ✔

--- Batch Run Complete ---
Status:  SUCCESS

title: Step 2 · Quantifying AMR with ResScan
section: 2c · Consolidate into one set of tables
text:
2c · Consolidate into one set of tables
Batch mode writes a folder per sample. resscan_aggregate pivots them into wide, analysis-ready tables — one file per metric, samples as columns:
resscan_aggregate \
    -s data/samplesheet.csv \
    -i SinkReplacementBatch \
    -o SinkReplacementBatchReports \
    -p SR
ls SinkReplacementBatchReports/ | head
You’ll get files like SR_homscan_RPKPMC.tsv, SR_homscan_RPKM.tsv, SR_varscan_RPKPMC.tsv, … — the exact shape the analysis uses. (On this subset they’ll be sparse; the full-depth versions are already in data/reports_full/, which Step 3 uses.)

title: Step 2 · Quantifying AMR with ResScan
text:
Tidy up
rm -rf work .nextflow*
mamba deactivate
You’ve quantified AMR the recommended way. Next, get to know the output in the output reference, or head straight to Step 3 · Analysis.

title: Reference · Understanding ResScan’s output
text: You’ve run ResScan. Now let’s read what it produced — the files, the columns, the metric names, and one word that trips everyone up: multiple. Keep this page open in a tab; it’s a lookup, not a lesson.

title: Reference · Understanding ResScan’s output
text:
What a run produces
A single resscan run makes one folder named after your -o prefix. Batch mode makes one such folder per sample. Inside:







File / folder
What it is




<prefix>_homscan.tsv
The main table. One row per detected AMR gene (homology models — whole-gene presence). All metrics as columns.


<prefix>_homscan_detailed.tsv
The same, but one row per read-to-gene hit — the raw evidence behind the summary.


<prefix>_varscan.tsv
AMR from point mutations — one row per resistance-conferring variant detected.


<prefix>_homscan_html/
Interactive per-gene coverage plots (open in a browser) — see where along each gene reads landed.


<prefix>_varscan_html/
The same, for the variant hits.


logs/, tmp/
Run logs and intermediates — safe to ignore (or delete).



The two .tsv files are what you analyse. The HTML plots are how you sanity-check a hit — a real gene shows reads spread along its length, not piled on one spot.

title: Reference · Understanding ResScan’s output
section: HomScan vs VarScan — both are genes
text:
HomScan vs VarScan — both are genes
This distinction confuses people, so plainly: both tables report genes. The difference is how resistance is detected.









HomScan (_homscan.tsv)
VarScan (_varscan.tsv)




Detects resistance by…
presence of a whole resistance gene (homology)
a specific point mutation in an otherwise-normal gene


CARD model
homolog model
protein-variant & rRNA-variant models


Typical example
KPC, TEM β-lactamases (the gene is the resistance)
gyrA S83L, 16S rRNA mutations (the mutation is the resistance)



So a fluoroquinolone-resistant E. coli carries a normal-looking gyrA gene — only a single base tells you it’s resistant. That’s VarScan’s job; HomScan would just see “a gyrA.” You want both.

Anatomy of an ARO id
Every row is keyed by a CARD ARO (Antibiotic Resistance Ontology) id. ResScan formats it so you can read it at a glance:
ARO_3002530__AAC_3_-Ib__H
ARO_3003411__Ecol_16S_TET__R__a964g
└──┬─────┘   └───┬────┘  │   └─┬─┘
 accession     gene name  │   mutation (a→g at position 964)
                          └─ model code
Model code — the trailing letter: H homolog · V protein variant · R rRNA variant · O overexpression · K knockout. H rows live in HomScan; the mutation-based codes drive VarScan.

title: Reference · Understanding ResScan’s output
text:
The columns
Both .tsv files share the same five annotation columns, then the metrics:







Column
Meaning




AMR_Gene_Family
The CARD family the gene belongs to (e.g. KPC beta-lactamase).


ARO
The ARO id (see above).


ARO_Name
Human-readable gene / variant name.


Drug_Class
Antibiotic class(es) affected — ;-separated if several.


Resistance_Mechanism
How it works (e.g. antibiotic inactivation).


metrics…
One column per abundance metric (next section).

title: Reference · Understanding ResScan’s output
section: The metrics — read the name, know the number
text:
The metrics — read the name, know the number
There are fifteen metric columns, but you don’t memorise them — you decode them. Every name is built from three parts:
 [ R | F ]  PK  [ '' | G | M | PC | PMC | PGC ]
   │        │      └─ what you divide by (the denominator)
   │        └─ Per Kilobase of gene length (always)
   └─ counting Reads or Fragments
Part 1 — Reads or Fragments. R… counts reads; F… counts fragments (a read pair = one DNA fragment). ResScan computes both families for every gene; the read-based metrics are the default — the per-cell RPKPMC below is the recommended headline number.
Part 2 — PK. Every metric divides by gene length in kb, so a long gene and a short gene are comparable.
Part 3 — the denominator — this is the one that matters:








Suffix
Divides by…
Answers




(none) — RPK/FPK
nothing else
raw length-normalised count


G — RPKG/FPKG
total gigabases sequenced
abundance per unit of data


M — RPKM/FPKM
total millions of reads/fragments
the classic metagenomics unit


PC — RPKPC/FPKPC
per bacterial cell (via single-copy genes)
copies per cell


PMC — RPKPMC/FPKPMC
per million cells
copies per cell, scaled ×10⁶


PGC — RPKPGC/FPKPGC
per billion cells
copies per cell, scaled ×10⁹



Plus two standalone columns: Read_Count / Fragment_Count (the raw tallies) and Lateral_Coverage_% (how much of the gene’s length was actually covered — your best single guard against a spurious hit).






TipWhich one should I use? RPKPMC



RPKPMC is ResScan’s preferred default metric: read-based, length-normalised, and scaled per bacterial cell against universal single-copy genes — so it’s comparable across samples of different depth and not thrown off by inflation from non-bacterial (e.g. human) reads. The M scaling just turns tiny per-cell fractions into readable numbers. This is the metric the analysis page uses, and the reason host removal is safe rather than sacred. ResScan still reports the full family of metrics above for anyone who needs them — a fuller account of why RPKPMC makes the best default is the subject of a separate, forthcoming paper.

title: Reference · Understanding ResScan’s output
text:
The word multiple
Short reads sometimes can’t be pinned to a single gene — a fragment matches several CARD alleles equally well. ResScan refuses to guess, and labels it multiple rather than arbitrarily crediting one gene. You’ll see it two ways:

In the ARO column: multiple[…] — the read hit several alleles, and the bracket lists exactly which ones (family;ARO pairs, |-separated). Fully transparent: you can see the candidates.
In the AMR_Gene_Family column: multiple — used only when even the family can’t be agreed on. If most of the tied alleles belong to one family (above a consensus threshold), ResScan keeps that family name and only the ARO stays multiple[…]; if they’re spread across families, the family itself becomes multiple.

Its metrics are still computed honestly (gene length is averaged over the tied alleles). Practically: a multiple row is real resistance you can trust at the family level (often even the specific family), just not resolved to one exact allele — usually a limit of read length, not of the tool.






WarningDon’t drop multiple rows



They’re genuine hits. In the sink data, multiple is one of the more abundant “families” precisely because closely related β-lactamase alleles are hard to tell apart from short reads — discarding it would throw away real signal.

title: Reference · Understanding ResScan’s output
text:
Batch mode: the aggregated tables
resscan_aggregate takes all those per-sample _homscan.tsv / _varscan.tsv files and pivots them into one file per metric, with the five annotation columns then one column per sample:
SR_homscan_RPKPMC.tsv               SR_varscan_RPKPMC.tsv
SR_homscan_Lateral_Coverage_%.tsv   … (one per metric, ×2 for hom/var)
That’s the shape the analysis reads: pick the file for the metric you want (RPKPMC by default), and every sample is already a column.

title: Appendix · Using your own data
text: You’ve run the whole workflow on a toy. Here’s everything that changes when you point it at real reads — plus the fixes for the snags people usually hit.

title: Appendix · Using your own data
text:
1 · Use the real human index
This is the one non-negotiable swap. The toy_human index that shipped with the repo is only the human mitochondrion — a stand-in so Step 1 runs in seconds. It removes almost no host DNA.






WarningNever run the toy index on real data



It will silently pass through the vast majority of human reads — into your results and, worse, into any files you archive. On real samples, always dehost against the full human genome.


Build a real host index once, then reuse it forever. Grab a decoy-aware human reference (T2T-CHM13 or GRCh38) and index it with the same bowtie2-build VANISH uses:
# ~3 GB download; the index build takes a while and needs ~16 GB RAM
wget -O GRCh38.fa.gz \
  https://ftp.ensembl.org/pub/release-110/fasta/homo_sapiens/dna/Homo_sapiens.GRCh38.dna.primary_assembly.fa.gz
gunzip GRCh38.fa.gz

bowtie2-build --threads 8 GRCh38.fa human_GRCh38
Then point VANISH at it instead of the toy — everything else in Step 1 is identical:
vanish --read_pairs read_pairs.csv \
       --fastq_dir /path/to/your/reads \
       --host_index human_GRCh38 \
       --cpus 8
Now the vanish_filtering_report.csv will show host removal doing real work.

title: Appendix · Using your own data
text:
2 · Bring your own reads
Two small things change for your own samples:

Mate naming. Tell vanish-prep how your files name their mates. Ours were _1 / _2; yours might be _R1 / _R2:
vanish-prep --fastq_dir /path/to/your/reads --r1 "_R1" --r2 "_R2" --out read_pairs.csv
Multiple runs per sample. If a sample was sequenced more than once, list all its reads on one samplesheet line — mates joined by commas, runs separated by semicolons:
SAMPLE_A,runX_R1.fq.gz,runX_R2.fq.gz;runY_R1.fq.gz,runY_R2.fq.gz
Pooling every run per sample is what makes the lateral coverage metric honest (see Step 2).

Everything downstream — resscan_batch, resscan_aggregate, the whole analysis — is unchanged. Same commands, your data.

title: Appendix · Using your own data
text:
3 · Keep the database current
CARD is updated regularly. To rebuild against a newer release, download it from card.mcmaster.ca and rebuild — same two steps as in Setup, just a new version string:
resscan_build_db -i CARD_raw -d resscan_CARD_v4.x.y
Record which CARD version you used with your results — resistome numbers aren’t comparable across database versions.

title: Appendix · Using your own data
text:
4 · Scale, cost, and cleanup

Threads vs. parallel. In resscan_batch, --parallel is how many samples run at once and --threads is cores per sample. Total cores used ≈ parallel × threads — set both to fit your machine, not beyond it.
Disk. Nextflow’s work/ directory grows fast and outlives the run. Delete it once you have the results you want:
rm -rf work .nextflow*
Environments. mamba deactivate when you’re done, and remove an env entirely with mamba env remove -n vanish-env (or resscan-env).

title: Appendix · Using your own data
text:
5 · Troubleshooting



Symptom
Likely cause & fix




command not found: vanish / resscan
The environment isn’t active — mamba activate vanish-env (or resscan-env).


environment.yml … pip install . fails
You must be inside the cloned repo when creating the env: ( cd tools/vanish && mamba env create -f environment.yml ).


VANISH removes ~0 host reads
You’re on the toy index. Build and use the real human index (§1).


ERROR: Samplesheet '…' not found
Path is relative to where you launched. Run from the repo root, or pass an absolute path.


Duplicate Sample IDs detected
Two rows share a sample_id. If it’s the same sample across runs, merge them onto one line with ;.


Per-sample ResScan tables are empty
Expected on the 10K subset — too shallow. Depth, not a bug (see Step 2).


Nextflow work/ filled the disk
rm -rf work .nextflow* after each successful run.


Analysis fold-changes look wrong / miss known genes
Aggregate per sample first, then average — don’t mean() over raw gene×sample cells (see Step 3).



That’s the whole workflow, toy to real. Clean reads in, calibrated per-cell numbers out, a resistome you can actually reason about.

title: Step 3 · Analysis — reading the resistome
text:
You’ve run the machinery. Now for the point of it all: what do the numbers say?
The story of these sinks, in four questions:

title: Step 3 · Analysis — reading the resistome
text:
Setup
library(readr); library(dplyr); library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2); library(forcats); library(stringr); library(vegan)

INT <- c(Before = "#4C72B0", After = "#DD8452")   # a consistent palette

meta <- read_csv("data/reports_full/metadata.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  rename(sample = 1) |>
  mutate(intervention = factor(if_else(Intervention == "Old", "Before", "After"),
                               levels = c("Before", "After")))

amr <- read_tsv("data/reports_full/SR_homscan_RPKPMC.tsv", show_col_types = FALSE)
amr is a wide table: one row per AMR gene, five annotation columns (AMR_Gene_Family, ARO, ARO_Name, Drug_Class, Resistance_Mechanism), then one column of RPKPMC per sample. Let’s melt it long and attach the metadata:
anno <- c("AMR_Gene_Family","ARO","ARO_Name","Drug_Class","Resistance_Mechanism")
long <- amr |>
  pivot_longer(-all_of(anno), names_to = "sample", values_to = "rpkpmc") |>
  left_join(meta, by = "sample")






ImportantRPKPMC — resistance per bacterial cell



RPKPMC is ResScan’s preferred default metric: resistance-gene copies per bacterial cell, calibrated against universal single-copy genes rather than against total reads. Because the denominator is bacterial cells, it stays comparable across samples of different depth and composition — which is also why the host-removal step pays off: stray human reads match neither the AMR genes nor the bacterial markers, so they can’t silently inflate or deflate the numbers the way they would with a total-reads metric like RPKM. ResScan reports a whole family of metrics alongside it (see the output reference); RPKPMC is simply the one to reach for by default.

title: Step 3 · Analysis — reading the resistome
section: 1 · How much? AMR load per sink
text:
1 · How much? AMR load per sink
Sum RPKPMC across all genes in a sample and you get its total resistance load — copies of resistance per cell, summed over every gene detected.
per_sample <- long |>
  group_by(sample, intervention) |>
  summarise(total_load = sum(rpkpmc), n_genes = sum(rpkpmc > 0), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(per_sample, aes(intervention, total_load, fill = intervention)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = .5, alpha = .85, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = .12, size = 2, alpha = .7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = INT) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_number(scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale())) +
  labs(title = "AMR load per sink", x = NULL, y = "Total RPKPMC (per cell)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) + theme(legend.position = "none")



AMR load per sink, before vs after


The median load more than tripled — roughly 332,000 → 1.19 million RPKPMC per sink. Replacing the plumbing didn’t reset the resistome; the new drains came back carrying more resistance per cell than the ones they replaced. (This is the headline of Kotay et al. 2025, reproduced from raw reads with your own hands.)

title: Step 3 · Analysis — reading the resistome
text:
2 · What kind? Composition shift
More resistance is one thing; different resistance is another. To ask whether the whole community’s makeup shifted, we put every sample in “resistome space” (each gene a dimension), measure how dissimilar samples are (Bray–Curtis), and squash that down to two dimensions with NMDS.
comm <- t(as.matrix(amr[, meta$sample]))     # samples x genes
set.seed(1)
nmds <- metaMDS(comm, distance = "bray", trace = FALSE)

sc <- as.data.frame(vegan::scores(nmds, "sites")) |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("sample") |>
  left_join(meta, "sample")

ggplot(sc, aes(NMDS1, NMDS2, colour = intervention)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = .9) +
  stat_ellipse(aes(group = intervention), linewidth = .4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = INT) +
  labs(title = "AMR community composition (NMDS, Bray-Curtis)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)



NMDS of AMR community composition


The two clouds overlap but pull apart — Before sinks sit left, After sinks shift right. So it isn’t only more resistance; the kind of resistance moved too. The overlap is the honest part of the picture: this is a shift in a noisy biological system, not a clean switch.

title: Step 3 · Analysis — reading the resistome
text:
3 · Which genes drove it?
Finally, name names. Roll RPKPMC up to gene family, average within each group, and rank families by how much they changed (log2 fold-change, After / Before).
fam <- long |>
  group_by(AMR_Gene_Family, sample, intervention) |>
  summarise(load = sum(rpkpmc), .groups = "drop") |>      # per-sample family total
  group_by(AMR_Gene_Family, intervention) |>
  summarise(mean_load = mean(load), .groups = "drop") |>   # then mean across sinks
  pivot_wider(names_from = intervention, values_from = mean_load) |>
  mutate(log2fc = log2((After + 1) / (Before + 1)),
         family = stringr::str_trunc(AMR_Gene_Family, 32)) |>
  slice_max(After + Before, n = 18)                        # 18 most abundant families

ggplot(fam, aes(log2fc, fct_reorder(family, log2fc))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#C44E52", width = .72) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  labs(title = "Top gene families: change after replacement",
       subtitle = "log2 fold-change (After / Before); 18 most abundant families",
       x = "log2 fold-change", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)



Top gene families by fold-change








WarningMind the aggregation



We sum genes within each sample first, then average across sinks — not one big mean() over every gene×sample cell. Average first and a family with many low-abundance genes gets washed out; the order of operations is the difference between seeing KPC at the top and missing it entirely.


Almost every abundant family rose, but two β-lactamases lead the board: TEM (log2fc ≈ 4.35) and KPC (≈ 3.67) — the carbapenem-resistance family behind much of the concern about hospital Klebsiella. Aminoglycoside families (ANT, AAC, APH) and efflux/MFS systems climbed too. A handful of environmental β-lactamases (BlaB, GOB, CME) went the other way — the incumbent drain community being replaced by a new one.

title: Step 3 · Analysis — reading the resistome
section: 4 · The resistance a gene catalogue can’t see (VarScan)

title: Step 3 · Analysis — reading the resistome
text:
The take-home
Four views, one conclusion: after the drains were replaced, the sink resistome came back larger (load tripled), different (composition shifted), clinically pointier in its acquired genes (KPC/TEM β-lactamases led the rise), and carrying more point-mutation resistance to fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, and fosfomycin (VarScan) — the last of which a gene-catalogue tool would never have seen. New plumbing, same problem — arguably worse.






NoteGo deeper



This is the teaching cut — four questions, four figures. The full study analysis carries the rest: per-variant VarScan detail, drug-class and resistance-mechanism breakdowns, per-room and per-period trends, and formal tests (PERMANOVA on the Bray–Curtis distances). The same tables in data/reports_full/ support all of it — the tools you’ve now run are all you need to get there.


Want to run this on your own samples? The Appendix covers the real human index, bring-your-own-reads, and cleanup.

title: ResScan Tutorial
text:
Hands-on tutorial · real ICU sink data
  Quantify AMR with ResScan.
  
    A step-by-step walkthrough on real hospital sink-drain metagenomes: clean your
    reads, quantify antibiotic resistance per bacterial cell, and
    watch a resistome rebound after the plumbing was replaced — in about
    15 minutes.
  
  
    Start the tutorial →
    See the analysis
  
  
    Built on the Kotay et al. 2025 ICU sink study
    Runs on Linux · macOS · WSL
    Free — no account, no cluster
  


What you'll build, in three steps


  
    1
    VANISH
    QC & host removal
    Quality-control every read and make the human DNA vanish — so you count
    microbes, not people.
  
  
    2
    ResScan
    Quantify AMR
    Map what's left against CARD and report resistance per bacterial
    cell — a metric that survives uneven depth.
  
  
    3
    R
    Analysis
    How much resistance, of what kind, driven by which genes — and see the
    resistome climb after the swap.
  


You'll do these in order — each step's page picks up where the
last left off. Begin with Setup.

What you’ll run it on

A bite-size slice of the real study — the first 10,000 read pairs from each of 36 sink-drain samples. Small enough to download in seconds and run on a laptop, yet enough to see every step work for real. The final analysis then uses the full-depth results (shipped with the repo), because that’s where the biology actually shows up.
New here? Start with the Overview for the story behind the data, or jump straight to Setup.




 Back to top

title: Overview
text:
Replace a contaminated hospital sink and you’d expect the antibiotic-resistance problem to go down the drain. It didn’t.
When Kotay et al. (2025, npj Antimicrobials & Resistance) ripped out and replaced the sink plumbing in six ICU rooms, the gleaming new drains were recolonised within weeks — and came back carrying more antibiotic resistance genes than the old ones, including mobile, clinically feared carbapenemases. The reservoir didn’t reset. It rebooted, worse.
How do you spot a surge like that in a soup of metagenomic reads? With the same two-tool workflow the study leaned on — and that’s exactly what you’ll run here.

title: Overview
text:
What you’ll do
Three short steps, start to finish:

VANISH — quality-control the reads and make the human DNA vanish.
ResScan — quantify the AMR genes that remain, normalised per bacterial cell.
Analysis — watch the resistome climb after the sinks were swapped.

title: Overview
text:
What you’ll run it on
A bite-size slice of the real study: the first 10,000 read pairs from each of the 36 sink samples. Small enough to download in seconds and run on a laptop — enough to see every step work for real.






NoteTen thousand reads is a keyhole view



Too shallow for meaningful biology, but perfect for learning the mechanics. So the final analysis step uses the full-depth results (provided) — that’s where the science actually shows up. The complete raw data lives on NCBI SRA under BioProject PRJNA587635.

title: Overview
text:
At a glance







You’ll need
Linux, macOS, or Windows (via WSL) · mamba/conda — we install everything else


Time
~15 minutes end-to-end on the subset


Footprint
The tutorial data is tiny; the toy human index ships prebuilt. (Real-world dehosting needs the full ~4 GB human index — covered in the Appendix.)


Cost
Free. No account, no cluster.



Ready when you are — head to Setup.

title: Setup
text: A little one-time housekeeping: two small Conda environments and one database. Nextflow and everything else come inside the environments, and the toy human index is already in this repo — so there’s no 4 GB download here. Budget ~10 minutes, mostly waiting for Conda.

title: Setup
text:
1 · Get the tutorial materials
Clone this repository and move into it — it’s your working directory for the whole tutorial.
git clone https://github.com/hsgweon/resscan-tutorial.git
cd resscan-tutorial
Inside, the teaching data is already prepared for you:







Path
What it is




data/rawdata_10K/
36 samples × 10,000 read pairs — the reads you’ll process


data/host_index/toy_human.*
Prebuilt toy human index (mitochondrion) — for dehosting


data/reports_full/
Full-depth results — used in the analysis step


data/read_pairs.csv
Ready-made VANISH input

title: Setup
text:
2 · Install VANISH
VANISH does the QC and host removal. Clone it and build its environment (this also installs the vanish commands):
git clone https://github.com/hsgweon/vanish.git tools/vanish
( cd tools/vanish && mamba env create -f environment.yml )

title: Setup
text:
3 · Install ResScan
ResScan does the AMR quantification. Same pattern:
git clone https://github.com/hsgweon/resscan.git tools/resscan
( cd tools/resscan && mamba env create -f environment.yml )






NoteTwo tools, two environments



You’ll use vanish-env for Step 1 and resscan-env for Step 2 — one at a time. Always run mamba deactivate before switching to the other, so you’re never in the wrong environment.

title: Setup
text:
4 · Build the CARD database
ResScan maps reads against CARD. Download it once and prepare it with ResScan’s builder. We pin v4.0.1 so your results line up with the full-depth reports used later. Activate resscan-env for this, then deactivate when done:
mamba activate resscan-env

wget https://card.mcmaster.ca/download/0/broadstreet-v4.0.1.tar.bz2
mkdir -p CARD_raw_v4.0.1
tar -xvjf broadstreet-v4.0.1.tar.bz2 -C CARD_raw_v4.0.1
resscan_build_db -i CARD_raw_v4.0.1 -d resscan_CARD_v4.0.1

mamba deactivate
This creates a resscan_CARD_v4.0.1/ folder — that’s the --card path you’ll pass to ResScan. It’s sub-gigabyte and takes a minute or two to build.

title: Setup
text:
5 · Quick check
Confirm each tool is installed. Activate, check, deactivate:
mamba activate vanish-env
vanish --help | head -3
mamba deactivate

mamba activate resscan-env
resscan --help | head -3
mamba deactivate
If both print usage text, you’re ready for Step 1.
